To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

articles.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
articles.summary: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents…
articles.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

articles.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
articles.summary: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time…
articles.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

articles.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
articles.summary: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in…
articles.abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.

articles.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
articles.summary: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context.
articles.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

articles.title: From syllable representation via gesture generation to articulation: A spiking neural model
articles.summary: Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural…
articles.abstract: Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Each syllable occurrence has a neural oscillator whose evolving phase coordinates its gestures and initiates the next syllable. Phase-dependent commands recruit separate neural populations for vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal actions (gestures). Neural ramp integrators shape the rise and fall of gesture activation. Together with articulatory targets, these trajectories determine the extent and time course of articulatory movements. Opponent neural populations provide control signals to a geometric articulatory model. Thirty reference recordings cover an input corpus of eight lexical words, an alternative realization of one word, a syllable sequence, and isolated syllables. Two additional paired simulation subcorpora of sixty runs each, covering two words and one syllable sequence, assess activation reliability across neural realizations. Adjusting gesture command amplitudes increased successful realizations from 57/60 to 60/60 under the specified criteria, with ramp rate factors held constant. The model demonstrates how neural oscillator and ramp dynamics generate articulatory timing under specified phasing rules. It complements a preceding mental-lexicon model through an ordered syllable interface. Continuous online execution across all components and connection to the acoustic extension remain further integration steps. Accessible code and synchronized visualization support inspection of the neural activation trajectories and resulting vocal-tract movements.

articles.title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
articles.summary: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are…
articles.abstract: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.

articles.title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
articles.summary: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has…
articles.abstract: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.

articles.title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
articles.summary: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where…
articles.abstract: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

articles.title: SPICE: Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments
articles.summary: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance…
articles.abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.

articles.title: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics
articles.summary: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from…
articles.abstract: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

articles.title: LuxTac: A Flexible, Scalable, and Open-Source Optical Taxel Array with Distributed Three-Axis Force Sensing for Tactile Robot Learning
articles.summary: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile…
articles.abstract: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile over a gripper. To solve this problem, we present LuxTac, a flexible, scalable optical taxel array, about 3.5 mm thick and built from off-the-shelf parts. Each taxel is a digital RGBC light-to-digital converter under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, so the back-scattered LED light falls monotonically with local indentation depth. The same board accepts two interchangeable gel cartridges: a plain one for normal sensing, and one with colored walls that encodes the local shear in the color of the returned light, with no camera, magnets, or bump overlay, making LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array to resolve shear at individual taxels. Characterized with an automated CNC indenter and a six-axis force/torque sensor, the normal cartridge responds linearly to force ($R^2$ = 0.999) from 104 mN to at least 5.8 N, with 2.0% repeatability, 5.9% hysteresis, and a taxel-to-taxel variation of 6-10% after normalization. With the shear cartridge, per-taxel models estimate the three-axis force at every taxel; across three indenter shapes and nine held-out sessions, the summed estimates reach $R^2$ = 0.96/0.96/0.92 in x/y/z, each taxel's estimate 0.92/0.93/0.94, and the median shear-direction error is 4.8 degrees. Adding LuxTac pressure readings to an Action Chunking Transformer policy substantially improves peg-in-hole success over a vision-only baseline. Design files, code, and videos are available at https://luxtac.github.io.

articles.title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
articles.summary: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar…
articles.abstract: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

articles.title: Learning the Dynamics of Deformable Linear Objects Through Coupled Oscillators for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
articles.summary: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their…
articles.abstract: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions. Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose $Φ$-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics. The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $Φ$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $Φ$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.

articles.title: RESCUE Jumper: A Centimeter-Scale Rolling and Jumping Robot for Search and Rescue
articles.summary: Centimeter-scale robots are promising for urban search and rescue because they can enter confined spaces that are inaccessible or unsafe for humans. However, their small size limits obstacle…
articles.abstract: Centimeter-scale robots are promising for urban search and rescue because they can enter confined spaces that are inaccessible or unsafe for humans. However, their small size limits obstacle traversal after deployment. This paper presents the RESCUE Jumper, a 125 g mobile robot with a 6.2 cm width and 6.2 cm diameter wheels that combines ground rolling with jumping to traverse steps and gaps that exceeds its rolling capability. The RESCUE Jumper uses its two actuators for both rolling mode and jumping by reversing the direction of wheel motion. Forward wheel motion enables rolling, while reverse wheel motion winds a spring steel tail to store elastic potential energy and release it for jumping. The RESCUE Jumper varies tail winding speed to control jump direction, transitioning from backward to forward jumps as winding speed increases from 0.75 rad/s to 8.73 rad/s. The launch angle of the jumps ranges from 45 degree to -11 degree with respect to the vertical axis, reaching a maximum height of 9.2 cm and a maximum lateral displacement of 11.2 cm. We model the winding speed-dependent jumping behavior in three phases: tail release to determine the contact point and robot orientation, tail straightening until liftoff, and ballistic flight to predict jump height and lateral displacement. Finally, qualitative tests highlight the robot's locomotion in cluttered, real-world environments. The model and experiments presented in this work can inform future designs of space-constrained jump mechanisms in centimeter-scale robots for search and rescue and inspection in unstructured environments.

articles.title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
articles.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is…
articles.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $π_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.

articles.title: Learning and Control in Physically Coupled Dynamical Systems
articles.summary: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and…
articles.abstract: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.

articles.title: BiCAT: Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization
articles.summary: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface…
articles.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.

articles.title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
articles.summary: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric…
articles.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.

articles.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
articles.summary: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human…
articles.abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

articles.title: Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency
articles.summary: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10…
articles.abstract: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.

articles.title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
articles.summary: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion…
articles.abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.

articles.title: Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling
articles.summary: The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model,…
articles.abstract: The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.

articles.title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms
articles.summary: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of…
articles.abstract: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.

articles.title: Expanding and Evaluating the Applicability of Safe Pareto Improvements
articles.summary: Even when players can make credible joint commitments in games, disagreement about the game's default outcome (e.g., about equilibrium selection) can prevent them from agreeing on any particular…
articles.abstract: Even when players can make credible joint commitments in games, disagreement about the game's default outcome (e.g., about equilibrium selection) can prevent them from agreeing on any particular payoff profile. We study safe Pareto improvements (SPIs): commitments that sidestep this obstacle by inducing a new game that is isomorphic to the original (after iteratively removing strictly dominated actions) but entrywise Pareto better. We do so by constructing token games: cheap-talk games rendered meaningful by commitments to take payoff-relevant actions (in prior work, strategies in the original game) as a function of the token outcome. Since these token games preserve the original game's strategic structure, players should expect them to be played isomorphically and hence agree that they Pareto improve on the original. In this work, we study token game SPIs under three additional commitment abilities: (1) burning utility, (2) transferring utility between players, and (3) transferring utility with an outside party conditional on the token outcome (e.g., via insurance-like contracts). We characterize when SPIs exist in each case and give efficient algorithms for optimizing over them. Finally, we propose evaluating SPI frameworks by how often they enable SPIs in randomly generated games. In such experiments, our methods substantially outperform prior work.

articles.title: Equilibrium Statistics and Stability in Random Two-Population and Three-Population Evolutionary Games
articles.summary: Multi-population matrix evolutionary games provide a framework for studying adaptation and strategic interactions among heterogeneous agents. When payoffs are uncertain, however, analysing a…
articles.abstract: Multi-population matrix evolutionary games provide a framework for studying adaptation and strategic interactions among heterogeneous agents. When payoffs are uncertain, however, analysing a specified game does not reveal how frequently different evolutionary outcomes occur or how their probabilities depend on modelling assumptions. We study two- and three-population games with two strategies per population and both within- and between-population pairwise interactions, with payoffs fixed during each evolutionary trajectory. For two populations, we derive equilibrium-existence probabilities and analytical stability results for generic games and three structured classes: diversity, exclusive, and avoidance games. For generic two-population games, independent Gaussian sampling of payoff entries and of replicator coefficients produces different equilibrium statistics. Interaction structure further distinguishes coexistence from attraction: diversity and exclusive games share the same interior-existence probability, but only exclusive games admit asymptotically stable interior equilibria. Avoidance games admit transversely attracting equilibrium families without locally asymptotically stable individual points. For generic three-population games under independent payoff sampling, we obtain existence probabilities for all equilibrium types and joint existence-and-stability probabilities for boundary equilibria. Monte Carlo simulations support the analytical predictions and quantify multistability, while phase portraits illustrate initial-condition dependence. Under the same Gaussian payoff-sampling protocol, simulations show a lower frequency of fully mixed equilibria but a higher frequency of multistability for three populations than for two.

articles.title: Computational Hardness of Online Stochastic Matching
articles.summary: In the online stochastic matching problem on a bipartite graph, offline vertices are given in advance, and online requests arrive sequentially from known distributions, each matched immediately and…
articles.abstract: In the online stochastic matching problem on a bipartite graph, offline vertices are given in advance, and online requests arrive sequentially from known distributions, each matched immediately and irrevocably to a free neighbor or rejected. Computational hardness results of the optimal online strategy have been known only for instances where online vertices have a fixed arrival order [Papadimitriou et al., 2024]. For random-order arrivals or even i.i.d. arrivals, it has been long open since the problem was proposed [Feldman et al., 2009]. In this paper, we give the first computational hardness results for online stochastic matching with random-order arrivals. In particular, we prove that for known i.i.d. arrivals, computing the online optimum is APX-hard, ruling out a Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme unless P = NP, even in unweighted graphs with two offline neighbors per online vertex. For random-order arrivals, even when there is only one offline node (i.e., the prophet secretary setting), computing the optimal online policy is #P-hard, resolving an open problem since [Dütting et al., 2023].

articles.title: A Common Exponential Lower Bound for Dantzig and Modified Simplex in Deterministic Discounted Games
articles.summary: On a family of $N$-state deterministic two-player discounted games, every run that chooses adaptively between Dantzig's rule and modified simplex requires $2^{Ω(N)}$ switches from a specified initial…
articles.abstract: On a family of $N$-state deterministic two-player discounted games, every run that chooses adaptively between Dantzig's rule and modified simplex requires $2^{Ω(N)}$ switches from a specified initial strategy, regardless of tie breaking. More generally, a return-gate construction lets Dantzig reproduce any finite Bland prefix in an undiscounted deterministic Markov decision process with rational rewards whenever every visited policy reaches a common sink from all states. Applied to an acyclic binary counter, deleting the minimizer's return actions preserves every fixed maximizing strategy's value at each original state while reducing Dantzig's switch count from exponential to linear. With returns, halving the total optimality gap can take $Ω(h/\log h)$ switches at discount horizon $h=(1-γ)^{-1}$, even on games solvable in linear arithmetic time. Conversely, Dantzig is strongly polynomial when strongly connected components have bounded size, each state has a bounded number of actions, and the condensation graph has height $O(\log N)$.

articles.title: Virtual Double Oracle: Faster Convergence by Leveraging Strategies That Were Watching All Along
articles.summary: Double Oracle (DO) and PSRO approximate Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games by iteratively expanding a strategy population with best responses supplied by an oracle. Online Double Oracle…
articles.abstract: Double Oracle (DO) and PSRO approximate Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games by iteratively expanding a strategy population with best responses supplied by an oracle. Online Double Oracle (ODO) interleaves multiplicative weights updates (MWU) with population discovery and obtains an $O(\sqrt{k\ln k/T})$ rate, where $T$ is the number of learning rounds and $k$ is the larger of the two players' final population sizes. We identify the reinitialisation step as an underexplored design choice: at each expansion, MWU-based methods reset newly discovered strategies to a uniform prior. We introduce Virtual Double Oracle (VDO), which exploits a bilinear identity (a strategy's full hindsight loss history collapses to its utility against the time-averaged opponent) to initialise each new strategy with the MWU weight it would have had from the start. We prove that VDO achieves $O(\sqrt{k/T})$ exploitability over the discovered population as it grows, provided the cumulative cost of adding strategies is at most linear in $k$, a condition supported by our empirical measurements. Discounted VDO (dVDO) moderates historical preferences to reduce over-concentration at reinitialisation. Experiments across matrix games, poker, and Goofspiel show that, with a suitable discount, dVDO can substantially reduce finite-horizon exploitability relative to both VDO and uniform-reset ODO, and can improve the discovered strategy populations.

articles.title: Exploiting Aggregate Feedback for Decentralized Equilibrium Learning in Markov Games: A Smart Grid Application
articles.summary: In many multi-agent systems, an agent's payoff depends on its own action and an aggregate of other agents' actions, rather than their individual decisions. This paper investigates decentralized…
articles.abstract: In many multi-agent systems, an agent's payoff depends on its own action and an aggregate of other agents' actions, rather than their individual decisions. This paper investigates decentralized equilibrium learning in Markov games (MGs) with such aggregative reward structures. However, existing decentralized learning algorithms for general MGs typically rely on bandit feedback, without exploiting the additional information available from aggregate observations. To exploit this information, we develop an aggregation-predictive stage-based V-learning algorithm with hybrid-feedback Exp3-IX. Using known local reward functions and observed aggregate quantities, each agent evaluates the immediate rewards of all candidate actions and predicts their immediate losses from historical aggregate feedback, while continuation values are learned from selected-action state transitions. The algorithm requires neither opponents' individual information nor knowledge of the transition kernel. We establish a high-probability regret bound that explicitly depends on aggregate prediction errors and retains the standard worst-case order. Under a regularity condition on adaptive stage lengths, the algorithm learns an $ε$-approximate coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) within $\widetilde O(SA_{\max}T^5/ε^2)$ episodes and extends to correlated equilibrium (CE) learning. We further apply the algorithm to a renewable-rich microgrid with strategic prosumers and shared energy storage. Numerical results show smaller deviation gaps and lower gap-AUC than three learning baselines. Compared with representative demand-response rules, the learned policies exhibit weaker incentives for unilateral deviations while maintaining favorable user rewards, high renewable utilization, and relatively stable electricity prices.

articles.title: Computing EF1 Allocations with Few Value Queries
articles.summary: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that allocates $m$ indivisible goods among $n$ agents with nonnegative additive valuations using $O(n^5\log^2 m)$ value queries and guarantees…
articles.abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that allocates $m$ indivisible goods among $n$ agents with nonnegative additive valuations using $O(n^5\log^2 m)$ value queries and guarantees envy-freeness up to one good (EF1). Concurrent work of Lin, Liu, Tao, and Zhou achieves $O(n^8\log m)$ comparison queries, attaining the optimal $O(\log m)$ dependence on $m$ for fixed $n$. Each comparison query can be simulated using two value queries, so their bound also holds for value queries. Our contributions are a much simpler algorithm and proofs, and polynomial-time computation.

articles.title: Settling the Time and Structural Complexity of Bertrand Networks
articles.summary: In the seminal Bertrand network game introduced by Babaioff et al. (2013), each seller posts a single price to captive buyers and to the markets it shares with neighboring sellers, where sellers…
articles.abstract: In the seminal Bertrand network game introduced by Babaioff et al. (2013), each seller posts a single price to captive buyers and to the markets it shares with neighboring sellers, where sellers cannot price discriminate across the markets. Although the existence of equilibria and polynomial-time algorithms to compute them in trees (Babaioff et al. (2013)) have been known, it has been a major open problem whether there exist efficient algorithms to compute them for general graphs. In this paper, we resolve this open question negatively by proving that computing any constant-error approximate Nash equilibrium in a Bertrand network is $\PPAD$-complete. This hardness holds even on sparse bipartite graphs of maximum degree five with constant integer market weights. Complementing our hardness result, we design an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS) when both the maximum degree and the number of sellers with captive buyers are bounded. Beyond time complexity, since exact equilibria require randomizing prices over continuous intervals, another fundamental question left open by Babaioff et al. (2013) is whether an exact equilibrium can always be represented with a finite number of price intervals, \ie whether its structural complexity is finite. We resolve this question affirmatively by proving that every achievable equilibrium revenue profile can be realized by an equilibrium with structural complexity $O(2^n)$, which leads to an exact algorithm running in doubly exponential time. We further show that this bound is tight: there exist instances for which the unique equilibrium realizing target revenue profiles has structural complexity $Ω(2^n)$.

articles.title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
articles.summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model…
articles.abstract: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

articles.title: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
articles.summary: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet…
articles.abstract: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

articles.title: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
articles.summary: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion…
articles.abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

articles.title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
articles.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as…
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

articles.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
articles.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of…
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

articles.title: NexSight: Verifiable Tasks for Fine-Grained Agentic Long-Video Understanding
articles.summary: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered…
articles.abstract: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.

articles.title: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation
articles.summary: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or…
articles.abstract: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.

articles.title: Out of Sight, Still in Mind: Token Compression for Omni-LLMs
articles.summary: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the…
articles.abstract: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the three streams is highly unbalanced: visual tokens account for the vast majority of the input, and are highly redundant. In this paper, we propose ReMo, a training-free framework that compresses visual tokens by redistributing their information across modalities: a visual token is kept only if its information appears nowhere else. ReMo achieves this in two ways: (i) it aligns audio and video in a shared space via closed-form calibration, and removes visual tokens already explained by the audio or by other visual tokens; and (ii) it replaces object-level visual tokens, identified by a lightweight object detector, with compact text proxies, short descriptions of each object and its location, conveying the same content in far fewer tokens. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two model scales, ReMo removes 54% of the input tokens with comparable accuracy. It performs comparably to the full-token model, reaching 101.2% and 101.4% of its average accuracy over five audio-visual benchmarks.

articles.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
articles.summary: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes…
articles.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

articles.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
articles.summary: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes…
articles.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

articles.title: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
articles.summary: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of…
articles.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

articles.title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
articles.summary: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic…
articles.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

articles.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
articles.summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon…
articles.abstract: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

articles.title: π^4: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
articles.summary: π^4 is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense…
articles.abstract: π^4 is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, π^4 achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation.
